text: Whoever takes the Son gets everything else with Him.
explanation:
A wealthy art collector lost his only son in war, and later commissioned a portrait of him. When the old man died, collectors flocked to the auction for his famous paintings. The first item was the son's portrait. No one bid, except the old family servant, who offered what little he had. The hammer fell, and the auctioneer announced the sale was over: the will said whoever took the son's portrait received the entire collection.

God has done the same. "He who did not spare His own Son… how shall He not with Him also freely give us all things?" Have the Son, and you have everything heaven holds.

text: On the Emmaus road, Jesus kept them from recognising Him so they'd see Him in the Scriptures instead.
explanation:
On His resurrection day, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples, but "their eyes were restrained, so that they did not know Him." Why not just show them His nail-scarred hands? Instead, "beginning at Moses and all the Prophets, He expounded to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself." Their hearts burned.

If they'd been lifted only by seeing Him in person, every generation after them would be at a disadvantage. But they were lifted by seeing Him in the Word, and you can see Him there too. When you're down, look for Jesus on every page.

text: Elijah didn't plead for Israel. Paul says he "pleads with God against Israel." God's answer was 7,000 faithful he didn't know about.
explanation:
After Mount Carmel, Elijah fled from Jezebel, collapsed under a broom tree and asked to die. God didn't scold him; He let him sleep and sent an angel to feed him, twice. But in the cave at Horeb, Elijah listed Israel's sins and said, "I alone am left." God replied, "I have reserved seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal," and told him to anoint his successor.

When we're burned out, it's easy to recount others' failings and imagine we're the only faithful ones left. God isn't impressed by either. And He wasn't in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still, small voice.

text: When there was death in the pot, Elisha didn't try to remove it. He added flour.
explanation:
During a famine, Elisha had a stew made for the prophets. One man, wanting to improve it, gathered wild gourds that looked good and sliced them in. As they ate, they cried, "Man of God, there is death in the pot!" Elisha said, "Bring some flour," threw it in, and "there was nothing harmful in the pot."

In this world, a little uncleanness spoils what's clean: a drop of sewage ruins a glass of the purest water. Only Jesus reverses it. When He touched lepers, they became clean; when He stepped into death, death had to leave. Bring Him into the situation.

text: The grain offering was fine flour: smooth, with no coarse grains. In Jesus, no trait ever overpowers another.
explanation:
Four of the five Levitical offerings picture Jesus' death; the grain offering pictures His life. It was fine flour: nothing coarse or uneven. He was truthful but kind, firm without being harsh, a servant washing feet but never servile. Oil was poured on it, as the Spirit led His every word; frankincense rose from it, as every deed pleased the Father.

The cakes were "mixed with oil" and the wafers "anointed with oil." He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in Mary's womb, and at thirty the Spirit came upon Him at the Jordan. When you need something to meditate on, try just two words: fine flour.

In a famine, a man brought Elisha twenty loaves of firstfruits bread. "Shall I set this before a hundred men?" the servant asked. Elisha said, "Thus says the Lord: they shall eat and have some left over," and they did. Jesus did the same, but bigger: over five thousand men fed, with twelve baskets left. And He didn't need to say "Thus says the Lord." He is the Lord.

When the disciples said, "This is a deserted place," they saw a wilderness. Jesus saw a storehouse. God's provision always exceeds the need; in your Father's house there's bread enough and to spare.

text: "We went through fire and through water; but You brought us out to rich fulfilment." Look for the way out: it leads higher than the way in.
explanation:
"You have caused men to ride over our heads." Sometimes, even with God's favour on you, people walk all over you, and it feels like fire and flood. But the psalm doesn't stop there. The word for "rich fulfilment" or "wealthy place" means saturation, overflowing abundance.

The only other place that word appears is Psalm 23: "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies… my cup runs over." The table is set in the middle of the battle, not after it. When the enemy attacks, keep your eyes on the Lord and come to His table. The way out leads somewhere higher than where you came in.
